speechtext: I notice by the papers that Premier Henry of Ontario has recently made a statement that the Prime Minister has intimated to him that it is the intention to introduce contributory unemployment insurance legislation. I wish to ask the Prime Minister if such an assurance has been given by him to Premier Henry, and if so, is it his intention to introduce such legislation this session?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot 'be responsible for what is said in the newspapers in any sense. I doubt very much whether the report accurately states what was said by Premier Henry. In common with other premiers he has discussed with me the question of unemployment insurance and it will be within the memory of the house that I made a statement as to what the result of the discussion was. Since that time the government has been engaged in endeavoring to ascertain to what extent, in view of the differences of opinion with respect to jurisdiction that existed, we could submit legislation to this house,. Whether or not it will be done at this session, I am not in position to state with any degree of absolute certainty. It may or may not and with respect to that I cannot say at the moment.

I do not know whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in using the word "that" was referring to my

Construction Camps
remarks as an interpretation of Premier Henry's statement or to the fact that Premier Henry had made a different statement. I should like to quote the dispatch itself, as follows:
"Mr. Bennett repeatedly has told me that contributory unemployment insurance is definitely coming," Mr. Henry declared. "He said he opposed non-contributory insurance, but he always suggested contributory unemployment insurance was inevitable."
The first part of the dispatch reads:
Canadian Press dispatch, Toronto, May 18.- Unemployment insurance on a contributory basis will be introduced by Premier R. B. Bennett in the near future, Premier George S. Henry of Ontario to-day told a delegation of women representing the Toronto and District Women's Unemployment Conference who asked the government for a provincial law as well as increased food and clothing relief allowances.
That is the exact wording of the dispatch to which I referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my answer covered the question asked by the right hon. gentleman. What I desired to make clear was that not only had it been discussed with Premier Henry but it had been discussed with the representatives of the provinces. There was a very full discussion and there is no doubt that I said to Mr. Henry what I said in this house and to the others, that I believed it was inevitable that some form of unemployment insurance would be enacted and that it should be on a contributory basis. There was some uncertainty as to the extent to which we might proceed to overcome the difficulties with respect to the provisions of the British North America Act and, as I say, I am not in position to-day to state definitely whether or not I shall endeavour to resolve those difficulties in a way which I think might be reasonable at this session.

speechtext: Yes-I beg my right hon. friend's pardon; might agree to act. May I reverse the question and ask the Prime Minister whether in his opinion a power conferred upon the provincial legislature under the British North America Act could, by the provincial legislatures, be delegated to the dominion in the first place or, secondly, would the provincial governments have power to ask the dominion to act as their agent with respect to the powers given them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I have no doubt as to
the right of the province to agree with the dominion that the dominion shall act as its agent or instrument to accomplish a purely provincial purpose. I am equally clear that the province would have no power to delegate part of its exclusive jurisdiction to the federal power. For instance, no one will question that the province might arrange by appropriate agreement that, we will say, a trust company should act to do certain work for it in connection with the exercise of its exclusive jurisdiction. If the dominion government were so minded it could agree to discharge these agency functions for the province at the request of the province, and there would be no doubt in my judgment as to the legality of such an arrangement. This bill contemplates that the cooperation between the federal power and the provincial power will be manifest wherever it is desirable, the federal power acting with the provincial power to accomplish a given end; and if it be necessary for the provincial power to act in cooperation with the dominion, the dominion may exercise to the full

its power. It does not propose to compel the province to do it, nor does it propose to compel the dominion, but it contemplates that as an instrumentality of government the province may agree to work with the dominion to accomplish a given end, and equally that the dominion may agree to cooperate with the province-the provincial authorities; I use the word province as covering all- for the same purpose. That is my understanding of the situation, and I think such power would be exercised in a perfectly legal manner.

speechtext: I can understand that if the dominion had enacted a law with respect to some matter and under that law wished the province to act as its agent in some particular it might have the power which the Prime Minister suggests. Under the subamendment I should say it would be quite proper to discuss anything that affects the particular recommendations that are to be made to the minister. If there is a poll, they will be made subject to that poll; if there is no poll, the regulations will be made in another way. It all comes back to the question of regulations. Before we proceed further it would be well for the committee to consider just where we are going in the matter of this proposed legislation. I should like to give the minister certain reasons why I think this and some other sections ought to be held over for further consideration before the committee is asked to support them. The regulations that are to be drafted and that are to become the law are to be made exclusively within the ambit of interested producers and the governor in council. Parliament does not enter into the picture at all. That is the first feature that I wish to make clear with respect to what this parliament is being asked to do. It is being asked to authorize certain interested groups combined with the governor in council to make what hereafter are to be the laws of the land. I say that that is an entirely wrong departure, that it amounts to what I have referred to before as a political revolution in the manner in which laws are hereafter to be made in this country. I do not think we ought to countenance such a step unless we are fully aware of where it is taking us in the matter of legislation.
The effort to get away from parliament is not new as other countries and other governments have been faced with similar difficulties. The parliament of Great Britain has to deal with a much larger number of subjects than this parliament, it has to deal with all the subjects which under our constitution are assigned to the provinces as well as to the dominion. That parliament has found it necessary to do a certain amount of delegating with respect to matters of legislation but in delegating powers to local bodies the parliament of Westminster very soon discovered that unless they were to depart entirely from the British constitution, to get away from the rule of law and the sovereignty of parliament it was necessary that some very clearly defined rules should be laid down within which it would be permissible for the minister to approve or disapprove of regulations, or for local bodies to be permitted to make regulations without the full approval of parliament with respect thereto. The Prime Minister of to-day has frequently directed the attention of this house to a volume which has been mentioned in the course of this debate- a work by the chief justice of Great Britain, Lord Hewart of Bury. The volume is entitled "The New Despotism." I doubt if hon. members have realized that this volume written by the Lord Chief Justice of Great Britain was written as a protest against the sort of thing we are here being asked to do at the present time, a protest so strong that the

Marketing Act
British parliament found it desirable to appoint a royal commission to report upon the whole question of delegated powers. I intend to read an extract or two from this work, and a paragraph or two from the report of the commission which submitted its findings to the British parliament, so that we may see how immediately those findings bear upon what is before this committee at the moment.
The situation as it presented itself to the Lord Chief Justice of England has been expressed by him in a paragraph in the introduction to this volume, under the title "The Nature of the Question." The author says:
The paradox which is in course of being accomplished is, indeed, rather elaborate. Writers on the constitution have for a long time taught that its two leading features are the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law. To tamper with either of them was, it might be thought, a sufficiently serious undertaking. But how far more attractive to the ingenious and adventurous mind to employ the one to defeat the other, and to establish a despotism on the ruins of both! It is manifestly easy to point a superficial contrast between what was done or attempted in the days of our worst kings, and what is being done or attempted to-day. In those days the method was to defy parliament-and it failed. In these days the method is to cajole, to coerce, and to use parliament-and it is strangely successful. The old despotism, which was defeated, offered parliament a challenge. The new despotism, which is not yet defeated, gives parliament an anaesthetic. The strategy is different, but the goal is the same. It is to subordinate parliament, to evade the courts, and to render the will, or the caprice of the executive unfettered and supreme.
The foregoing appears at page 10. I contend that every line of that paragraph is borne out by what has been happening in this committee since the introduction of this measure. It is perfectly clear that the tendency of this legislation is to get away from the supremacy of parliament in the making of laws, to get away from the rule of law as determining the rights of subjects throughout the entire dominion. Perhaps I had better refer to an earlier page in this volume where Lord Hewart says:
The citizens of a state may indeed believe or boast that, at a given moment, they enjoy, or at any rate possess, a system of representative institutions, and that the ordinary law of the land, interpreted and administered by the regular courts, is comprehensive enough and strong enough for all its proper purposes. But their belief will stand in need of revision if, in truth and in fact, an organized and diligent minority, equipped with convenient drafts, and employing after a fashion part of the machinery of representative institutions, is steadily increasing the range and the power of departmental authority and -withdrawing its operations more and more from the jurisdiction of the courts.
i.Mi. Mackenzie King.'
That is exactly what is proposed by this very section; it is to take away from parliament first of all the making of the law, to put the laws governing the regulation and marketing of products into the hands of occupational groups in local areas who, in order to have their regulations become law, shall be subj ect only to the approval of the governor in council. And such regulations are to be given their widest scope in some instances subject only to the approval of the minister. It begins and ends outside of the ambit of parliament altogether.
Now I say that legislation of the kind should not be countenanced by this parliament for one moment. It is not necessary to get away from the authority of parliament, it is not necessary to do away with the making of laws in accordance with the practice and procedure of this House of Commons, in order to give the farmers of this country or any other class what is needed in full to safeguard their interests and to improve their condition where that is possible.
I have referred to the action of the British parliament in appointing a royal commission to study the whole question of the delegation of powers. I have in my hand the report of that commission on ministers' powers. Report Presented by the Lord High Chancellor to Parliament by Command of His Majesty, April 1932. The report states that the committee was appointed:
to consider the powers evercised by or under the direction of (or by persons or bodies appointed specially by) ministers of the crown by way of (a) delegated legislation and (b) judicial or quasi-judicial decision, and to report what safeguards are desirable or necessary to secure the constitutional principles of the sovereignty of parliament and the supremacy of the law.
That was the purpose for which the commission was appointed. Now what does this commission say as to the essentially subordinate character of delegated legislation? I would suggest to hon. members that they read carefully the entire report, but this one section bears immediately on the legislation which is before us at the moment-this section with regard to the essentially subordinate character of delegated legislation. All this legislation that is left to the local boards to be approved of by the governor in council is delegated legislation, and with respect to delegated legislation this royal commission has reported that certain safeguards should be thrown around such legislation, safeguards wholly lacking in this measure. In that regard may I read one paragraph which appears at page 20:

Marketing Act
The power to legislate, when delegated by parliament, differs from parliament's own power to legislate. Parliament is supreme and its power to legislate is therefore unlimited. It can do the greatest things; it can do the smallest. It can make general laws for a vast empire; it can make a particular exception out of them in favour of a particular individual. It can provide-and has in fact provided-for the payment of old age pensions to all who fulfil the statutory conditions: it can also provide-and has in fact provided

for boiling the Bishop of Rochester's cook to death. But any power delegated by parliament is necessarily a subordinate power, because it is limited by the terms of the enactment whereby it is delegated.
It is a princijjle of our constitution that whatever laws are passed by parliament are binding, as the law of the land, on everybody. But it is also a principle of our constitution that no one may be deprived of his liberty or of his rights except in due course of law-i.e., unless he has done something which the law says specifically shall have that effect. In the absence of a common law or a statutory authority, "A" cannot be deprived of rights by an executive act of a minister; and if the minister claims to have made a regulation entitling him to interfere with "A's" rights, the courts will interfere to stop the minister unless he can show by what authority, statutory or otherwise, he has made the regulation in question.
It follows, therefore, that to safeguard the second of the two principles just mentioned the precise limits of the law-making power, which parliament intends to confer on a minister, should always be defined in clear language by the statute which confers it.
There is nothing here in the nature of statutory law, nothing that may be cited as law, to which all persons in the country will be subject. The very essence of this proposed legislation is that there shall be one law for one locality and another law for another, that the producers in one province may have one scheme and the producers in some other province another. These schemes, not if they receive the approval of parliament, not if they find existence in a statute or a resolution approved by parliament, but simply if sanctioned by the governor in council, are to become the law of the land. That is a very serious departure from anything that has been done or attempted in this parliament heretofore and I hope the minister, before he asks the House of Commons to commit hara-kiri so far as its functions are concerned and, with respect to marketing legislation, to turn over the whole business to occupational groups to be subject only to the approval of himself and his colleagues in council, will consider where that tendency, that particular step, is going to land this country in the matter of its legislative enactments.
The other day I was pointing out that in other parts of the world certain tendencies
are at work which are wholly subversive of political institutions, for instance, the tendency in Russia where parliaments are ignored and the matter of legislation left to the regulations of occupational groups to determine according to their self interest, regardless of the people as a whole who may nevertheless be vitally affected by much of the regulatory legislation there enacted. There is the further tendency in Italy, Austria and Germany where one individual or a group that has authority for the moment may take advantage of that authority to say what the regulations are that are to govern. Both of those tendencies are wholly subversive of all that British parliamentary institutions stand for, and yet by this legislation we are being asked to endorse each of these two tendencies. We are being asked first of all to allow the making of certain laws to be left in the hands of self interested class groups and to leave to an interested minister to say whether or not their particular scheme is to be approved. If I wished to take up the time I could quote from this volume paragraphs which state that in any case where any matter of a judicial or quasi-judicial character is left to a minister for approval, care should be taken to see that the minister to whom the matter is left is not a minister of the crown who may by any chance be interested in the particular subject that is being brought before him. They make the following specific recommendations with regard to judicial or quasi-judicial decisions such as would have to be made where a scheme was accepted and where all the parties to a scheme may have a voice:
We, therefore, make the following specific recommendations:-
I.	Judicial, as distinct from quasi-judicial, functions should normally be entrusted to the ordinary courts of law, and their assignment by parliament to a minister or ministerial tribunal should be regarded as exceptional and requiring justification in each case.
II.	Where parliament considers it necessary to depart from the normal course, it should entrust the judicial functions involved in the legislation to a ministerial tribunal rather than to the minister personally. The appointment of such a tribunal may be left to the minister, but the tribunal should be independent of him in the exercise of their functions. In regard to the more important jurisdictions so set up, the Lord Chancellor should be consulted before appointments are made.
Assignment to a ministerial tribunal rather than to the minister would clearly be right in any case where it appears likely that the minister (in which word we include any officer of the department acting under his orders) would be likely to be precluded from acting as a judge by the kind of departmental "interest" described in paragraph 3.
Judicial functions should not be entrusted to the minister personally unless there is some
very special and exceptional reason for that course and even in that event not where there is "interest" of the kind last mentioned.
III.	Quasi-judicial decisions fall naturally to ministers themselves and not to courts of law or ministerial tribunals. But in any exceptional case in which it appears probable that a minister may be disqualified by an "interest" of the kind last mentioned from discharging impartially the judicial functions involved in the quasi-judicial decision, parliament should consider the desirability of dividing the decision and entrusting the judicial functions to a ministerial tribunal whose adjudication would be binding on the minister when in his discretion he completes the quasi-judicial decision by administrative action.
IV.	Before the decision is given, whether it be judicial or quasi-judicial, each of the parties to a dispute should be given the opportunity of stating his case (not necessarily orally) and also of knowing the case which he has to meet and of answering it if he can.
V.	Every minister exercising a judicial or quasi-judicial function and every ministerial tribunal exercising a judicial function should give the decision in the form of a reasoned document.
This document should be available to the parties.
In making this quotation I am anticipating somewhat what is provided for in some of the other sections of this bill, but which very properly come in for consideration at this moment because they have to do with the power of making and determining offences. They may have their licences taken away if they do not abide by decisions with respect to regulations made, and there is no opportunity to appeal or even of being heard by way of protest. There is no reasoned argument given as to why one man should be treated in one way and another man in another; the whole matter is left to be dealt with in the arbitrary fashion to which reference already has been frequently made.

Before the amendment is carried: earlier in the afternoon I asked who would be entitled to vote if a vote were decided upon. I recognize the difficulty of the situation that may arise when a certain group or industry wishes to come under the provisions of the act. There is nothing in the bill to define who is entitled to vote when a vote is decided upon. In the fourth line of the amendment it says: "or may require that a poll be taken." Taken by whom, of whom? There can be so many different kinds of polls and so many methods of having a vote that I think parliament has a right to know the method the minister has in mind when he decides that a vote is to be taken. For instance, it may be only the producers in the industry that will be in favour of a vote. As a concrete example take, the tobacco growers: supposing .they petition the government to come under some scheme, who among the tobacco growers will vote? I cannot imagine that anyone outside those interested in the industry will be entitled to vote. I believe that under the bill now before us we are setting up a form of economic councils within industries. When the tobacco industry is being considered I do not expect the apple growers to vote. Therefore in spite of the objections that have been taken I still feel that it is proper that a particular economic group shall have the say as" to the form of organization and the future course that the industry shall take.
.Then will the vote be limited to Canadian citizens? In an industry you may have half a 
dozen different nationalities. We have no indication from the government as to that. Will companies be entitled to vote, or will it be determined, for instance, by quantity of production? In a given industry in which 500 people may be engaged, perhaps ten out of the 500 may have more than 50 per cent of the production; will those ten have more say than the rest? I think these points ought to be clarified, otherwise I would prefer to see the clause stand until something is put in to determine who shall have the right to vote when a vote is decided upon.

They will be able to suggest the beat and simplest way of taking a poll, also who will be entitled to vote, and who will be exempt. There is just one point which has not been mentioned in regard to the amendment proposed by the minister. As the minister has said, it will be largely left to the producers themselves in their submitted schemes to say whether or not a vote shall be taken and how that vote shall be carried out. This goes a little further, however; upon receipt of a report from the board recommending the approval of a scheme as constituted or amended by the board, the minister may recommend approval thereof; or in lieu of recommending approval, if he is not satisfied that those applying are representative of the industry, for example, or if the scheme does not suggest a vote, the minister may provide that a vote shall be taken. Then it is no longer a matter of the producers having said whether or not a vote shall be taken; if the minister is not satisfied that those who present the scheme are truly representative he, not the board or the producers, may state that a vote shall be taken, and he may lay down the conditions under which that vote shall be taken.

I want to submit to the minister that surely he and his staff, the government and this house, can decide better than a number of growers in a district as to who should vote, and I think that should be done before this bill goes through. That is my submission. It may be that we are facing great difficulties, but surely it is easier for us to solve those
difficulties than it is for the people in the locality to do so when they are confronted with all the difficulties and differences that may and I think are bound to arise in an attempt to work out a scheme such as this.
I just want to refer the minister to the fact that in other cases of local control we have votes. For instance, in regard to whether or not a drainage scheme shall be installed in a certain locality, a vote is taken. The legislature that gave the authority to take that vote says who shall vote. If a local assessment such as a sidewalk is to be constructed, surely no legislature would think of omitting to define who shall vote on the question of whether or not that local improvement shall be proceeded with. I think that is absolutely a parallel case. Then take the matter of building restrictions; the local legislature defines who shall vote on a question of that kind, and the same thing applies to the way the affairs of a school section are run. Do you suppose any legislature in the land ever left it open to the people who came to the meeting to decide who should or should not be the electors? There can be no question about it; if you propose to have a vote at all you must define who are to be allowed to vote. You are simply creating uncertainty and difficulty otherwise, and increasing the opportunities for friction. It may take a little time and labour, but surely this is the tribunal to decide that matter, and I think it should be decided before this bill is passed.

But if the provisions respecting the administration of the act are too loosely drawn up; if the law is not placed on a proper basis, I have grave fears as to the outcome of the legislation itself. I regard the administration of the act as almost of more importance than the act itself, because the benefits the producers may derive from it depend entirely upon how the act is administered. One of the important features of the aot is the creation of these boards, and naturally some importance must be attached to the question who is entitled to vote on these schemes that are to be proposed to the central authorities.
I can understand the position of the minister when he says that a certain amount of flexibility is required in the drawing up of this measure on account of its experimental nature, but undoubtedly the minister has given considerable time and study to how the act is likely to be administered and the way in which the boards are to be created, and he has not yet given the committee the benefit of his continuous research into the provisions of this measure.
Just prior to six o'clock I pointed out how many different angles there are to the question of who is entitled to vote. There is no definition in the bill itself of what constitutes a poll; at least I have not been able to discover it. Perhaps it may be done by a show of hands, perhaps by secret ballot, perhaps by mail or some other means. Up to now we have had no information from the minister as to what he regards a proper definition of the term poll.
If this clause is to operate on the basis of the method suggested by the minister it is quite possible that a meeting will be called. How that meeting is to be called I cannot say; who will be authorized to call a meeting I do not know. Let us assume for a moment that a meeting is called in a schoolhouse in some agricultural community and that seventy-five or a hundred people attend the meeting. You might well have seventy-five different opinions as to who is entitled to vote on the scheme. Somewhere a guiding principle should be laid down so that the people who come to the meeting will know for what purpose it is called; otherwise you might have a large number of men and women attending the meeting and desiring to come under the act, and then, after considerable discussion and deliberation, going away without anything definite being done. In that respect this act is the same as the British act, and evidently to a certain extent for the same reason. The hon. member asks why we do not state in the bill who shall vote and who shall not. It is the producers who submit a scheme after giving it careful consideration who are in the best position to recommend who shall be exempted from the scheme, and those who are exempt would not necessarily have a vote. Outside of that, every producer within the area defined would have a vote. What the hon. member is asking us to do is this: He wants us to decide in this committee who shall be exempt from the operation of a scheme proposed, let us say, by the tobacco growers of Ontario, or in connection with the dairy industry; whether a man should be exempt if he had two milk cows, or three or four; and the same thing in connection with the lumbering industry. It might also apply to the fish industry. I am sure the hon. member is sufficient of a business man to realize that it is impossible for us to take up the time of the house in this committee in an attempt to do that. This matter has been given very careful consideration and I think it will appeal to the good judgment and common sense of everyone that it would be impossible for us in this committee to go into all these matters in detail. The British act, realizing the same difficulty, deals with the matter in a similar way. The scheme submitted might deal just with export or interprovincial trade.
If it will be of any assistance to the hon. member I would say that in my judgment when the producers submit their scheme they will state in it who are to be exempt and the conditions upon which producers will be exempt. Then after full consideration they ask for a poll, and if the majority vote is in favour of the scheme, the whole scheme will be published and everything in connection with it will be known. So that the difficulty my hon. friend feels might arise in a meeting in a schoolhouse would be avoided because what they were coming to discuss would be known to everyone attending.

The amendment which has just been moved helps to emphasize what I wish to say about this particular clause. It seems to me that this so called marketing bill is in reality two separate measures welded into one. One measure is based on some theory of economic nationalism while the other is based on some theory of economic imperialism. The one dealing with economic nationalism undertakes to bring into being a number of local boards which will have the approval of the governor in council to regulate marketing within the dominion. As we have just seen by the clause last passed, the process is to start with a local board, have it make certain regulations and then enlarge the scope of those regulations by allowing the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister to make regulations just as wide as possible We come now to a new departure. If no local board has moved in the matter and the governor in council has not taken any steps as a consequence of any local action, the governor in council may be moved into action from some other source or direction. It is this other source or direction which I think needs to be considered in connection with this section and section number 12. Section 12 gives the governor in council the power to prohibit altogether certain importations into Canada and certain exportations from Canada. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but my understanding of clause 9 is that it is designed to further not a Canadian marketing scheme but an empire marketing scheme. It is the means whereby under an arrangement that has been come to among certain gentlemen in different parts of the empire we are hereafter to have the products of the empire regulated by some central authority in London which will be either visible or in-

Marketing Act
visible. The reason I feel quite so sure of my ground as I do is this. I have in my hand at the moment a marketing scheme from the imperial point of view as set forth by no less prominent an organ of the empire than the London Times. It all relates to this bill before the house and explains its imperial significance. Several editorials on the subject have in fact appeared in the Times, the first of which was published on April 3 of this year. It is entitled "Planned Empire Markets." It explains how this present bill which is before this parliament and which it says is likely to be the one to create most discussion in this house, is to fit into an empire marketing scheme whereby an arrangement for complementary production and trade is to be carried out within the empire. The editorial of April 3 was followed by another of considerable length on "The Empire and the British market." This appeared in the Times of April 25. There is another one relating to this same subject in the Times of March 14, under the title "The Empire Group", and still another editorial on May 3 entitled "Mr. Bruce's mission."
As we know, the Right Hon. Mr. Bruce is to be here next week, and I have been wondering whether one of the reasons we are not sitting on Thursday of this week, as the house has sometimes done before, and why the business of the house is being protracted as it is, is to enable Mr. Bruce and the Prime Minister of Canada and others to see what further action if any can be taken in regard to empire marketing before the question is finally determined. Let me read a paragraph or two from the Times editorial of April 3: entitled "Planned Empire Markets."
The Natural Products Marketing bill which the Canadian government has introduced into the federal parliament seems likely to become the principal issue in dominion polities.
It is significant that the London Times had that view before the bill was discussed in this house, because it was well after April 3 before we began the consideration of the measure here. The measure itself was introduced only on the eve of the Easter recess and not given second reading till some time after. The editorial goes on to say how the bill is likely to be received. I quote:
It provides the framework within which they can organize their own marketing scheme, the success of which will depend upon their capacity for effective cooperation. The wide sweep of the measure has come as a surprise in Canada, and has caused some alarm among business men, especially among those engaged in buying and selling commodities. On the other hand, it is welcomed by the farmers, 74726-206
who are principally concerned, and it appears that most of the provincial governments are ready to cooperate by passing the necessary supplementary legislation. Canada depends upon her primary production, and most of her farmers, like those of Great Britain, seem to have become convinced by recent experience that unlimited competition is incompatible with security.
Then it says that this bill is avowedly modelled on the British measure, though there may be certain features taken from the American experiment in economic planning. It then proceeds:
If it becomes law and is put into effective operation, Canadian farmers will be organized on the same lines as the British, and the discussion of common problems and the arrangement of satisfactory conditions for mutual aid will be proportionately easier. A similar development seems likely in Australia. Mr. Bruce's experience in London has convinced him more than ever that the economic salvation of the commonwealth, and indeed of all the British countries, depends on the pursuit by the governments of the empire of a concerted policy in trade and production, and not by the governments alone, but also by the leaders of agriculture, industry, commerce, and finance. If however, these leaders are to conclude effective agreements with one another, it can only be as the responsible spokesmen of organized bodies representing the different sections of the national economy.
There you will find the real reason for this bill. It is not the local marketing features that will be really significant as this measure begins to be operative, but the extent to which the production and trade of this country are to be made subject to some enonomie empire planning scheme of which so far as Canada is concerned no one but the governor in council himself will have precise knowledge. Under this section parliament is asked to leave in the hands of the governor in council, without discussion in this house, the scheme which is to govern in regard to production and trade in Canada, a scheme which through the agency of empire government is to form part of a concerted policy in trade and production. It is time that we considered carefully what this government may do with respect to imperial marketing schemes before allowing the government to have the authority given it by this proposal.
I could quote from the other editorials I have mentioned to show that the whole matter is one that has been carefully thought out in London and is undoubtedly worked out in different parts of the empire through the cooperation of interested parties. What I wish to take exception to is not that the ministry should have a plan of empire marketing, if that is what they deem to be desirable, but

Marketing Act

that they do not come forward and state frankly that such is their policy. I take exception to the fact that under the guise of a bill which purports to regulate production and trade in the interests of the farmers of Canada, the farmers may find themselves eventually in the position where they must discover that unwittingly they have been supporting some thing which gives the governor in council in Canada the power to prevent altogether the exportation of some of their products and equally the power to prevent altogether the importation into Canada of commodities which they may find it very much in their interest to have imported. That is the really serious aspect of the bill, and I submit it is a consideration of which this house should take very full account before it sanctions the passing of section 9.

It might have been easily arranged to have these cattle, by means of a system of credit or by some arrangement in conjunction with the provinces, moved to districts where there fMr. Mackenzie King.1
was sufficient feed. The farmers in those districts might not have enough money, but if they had been given assistance in the purchase, in the form of credit, they could have marketed their product to much better advantage than they did.
Another instance in which this might be used to a greater extent is illustrated by the experiment we carried out this past fall in the shipping of feeder lambs and ewes from ranges in the west to the farmers of Ontario. It has worked out very satisfactorily. Under present arrangements these ranchers will ship the lambs to the stockyards and pay local freight. Then there are additional charges, handling charges in the stockyard and also the losses that come from keeping stock like that for a number of days in conditions to which they are not accustomed. Then they are bought, loaded and shipped to Ontario, as in this case they might have been, and another local freight is charged. They are shipped to Toronto and left there where further charges are made upon them. Then there is another local freight charge to the farmers in Ontario. I believe that would not happen if that particular industry were organized, but until it is, that is one instance in which I think the marketing board would take the lambs from the ranchers in this way and as we did take them, with one local freight to the farmers in Ontario who wish lambs for feeding, not only saving the farmer a great deal of actual outlay but bringing the lambs to them in better shape. The same thing might be done by the dominion board being the connecting link, if that were necessary, between the provincial marketing board in Alberta or Saskatchewan and the one in Ontario.
Similarly as regards our cattle, it would have saved many dollars to the Ontario people and also to the western people if the cattle had been contracted for under supervision and with a guarantee of quality and grade to the Ontario farmers, and shipped directly rather than through the stockyards, w'here, no matter what care is taken, farmers have in many cases experienced losses from haemorrhagic septicaemia.
Also with regard to coarse grains a great deal of regulatory work could be done until the industry had an opportunity to organize. At the same time a case like this might arise: In 1930 or 1931, when we were forced to ship our cattle to the United Kingdom and it was necessary, in doing so, to put before the old country farmers the best type of cattle we had to export, there did not seem to be any action

Marketing Act
taken by private individuals to make such shipments and I was able personally by calling in five or six of the largest ranchers in the west to persuade them even to take a loss, if that were necessary, to fit up certain boat loads of cattle of that type to ship to the feeding farmers in the old land. The ranchers felt at the time that they were going to lose a good deal on this shipment, but as the matter turned out their cattle met with such approval in the old land they netted back to the ranchers in Calgary and Moose Jaw considerably more than they were offered before the cattle were shipped. In that case it was possible to carry that out by making that arrangement. I believe it would have been better if we could have continued to make such trial shipments to the old country, and especially if we have reason to believe they wish live stock of a certain type-and I will take live stock because I have been dealing with it-this board could make points of contact in this way more advantageously than could be done by a great deal of advertising such as is being carried on by other countries.
The same procedure might be carried out in regard to other countries where we felt that we could establish new channels of trade. In that connection I might, say that there is and has been for the past two or three years quite a good possibility of this, but no advantage seems to have been taken of it because no person has before him the picture as a whole. I have reference to the demand that could be created in the United Kingdom for malting barley, barley of the malting type. We put on an exhibition there and our barley met with the highest approval by the old country maltsters. They made inquiries but found that no uniform supply was coming forward. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and northern Alberta are particularly well adapted for the production of this kind of barley. I use this simply for an illustration. If we could follow up this exhibition that has been put on from year to year for at least four years-because it had been put on before I took over the portfolio I hold-we could assist very much and perhaps start a new trade to be handed ov^r, if the industry itself did not become organized, to private interests. That, in my opinion, will avoid a good deal of confusion, but there is one phase which is dealt with under the amendment and which I believe is one of the most important in the whole picture. We have referred in the house before to those small exportable surpluses of so many types of farm products which, although small, are able to smash and disorganize the entire domestic price. It is sometimes impossible for the average exporter to get rid of this surplus by exporting it, because he could do so only at a loss, and because the prices in outside markets during certain periods of the year are lower than the Canadian price. The result is that those surpluses remain here and disorganize and bring to chaos the domestic price, even though they amount to perhaps only five per cent of the whole. Where such a situation exists, not only is the minister empowered through order in council to bring into effect a scheme to take care of export matters, but the dominion board is, under this amendment, empowered to act as that exporting agency or to appoint an exporting agency. In other words, it provides the machinery through which this small exportable surplus, be it cattle, hogs, dairy products, eggs or what not, may be taken off the domestic market, thus stabilizing it; and if and when losses are involved by export it will provide that the entire trade may contribute to make up those small losses. That to my mind is very important; without it the bill would fail of at least half its purpose. I heartily approve the amendment as brought down.

Certainly this is a usurpation of the rights of parliament, as complete as anything could be. Let me read the section:
12 (1) The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette, restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product which enters Canada in competition with a regulated product, and the governor in council shall have power to make regulations to provide for the licensing by the minister of importers, or otherwise to enforce any order made hereunder.
(2) The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette,-
(a)	provide that any natural product shall not be exported from Canada without a licence;
(b)	prescribe the forms of such licences, the terms and conditions thereof and the persons who shall have authority to issue the same;
(c)	impose penalties for breach of any such order or regulation or of any licence issued thereunder, and, generally, make such provision or authorize the doing of such acts or things as may in his discretion be deemed necessary or expedient for giving full effect to any orders, regulations or licences made or issued hereunder.
In a word, Mr. Chairman, if that section began with the words "the parliament of Canada" I would have no exception to take to it. Then we would have power in this parliament to say whether or not any, and if any, what restriction of trade should take place; whether or not the imports of this country should be restricted and, equally, the exports. I do submit that the constitution of this country, the British North America Act, gives no such power to the governor in council, and it cannot be construed that because exclusive power is given the federal parliament to legislate on matters of trade and commerce this parliament can take those powers in their entirety and transfer them to the governor in council. Let me read section 91 of the British North America Act:
It shall be lawful for the Queen-
Not the governor in council.
[DOT]-by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the fore-

going terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the clases of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
2. The regulation of trade and commerce.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is only
this parliament that can pass laws for the regulation of trade and commerce to the extent of restricting exports and imports, and under the constitution parliament has not the power to delegate that right of legislation to the governor in council. Much less has it the right to interfere in matters that come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The provinces have exclusive jurisdiction. to legislate with respect to property and civil rights; surely they have some say with regard to the licensing of the citizens within the provinces who are carrying on their ordinary vocations and occupations. This section states that at the instance of the governor in council any producer in Canada may be obliged to take out a licence before he can sell a product or offer it for sale. That comes to the same thing as not being allowed to produce, because if a man is not permitted to sell or offer for sale the things he produces very soon he will cease to produce without a licence. A producer becomes liable under this section to a penalty of fine or imprisonment at the instance of the governor in council for pursuing what up to that moment has been his only source of livelihood, his only occupation.
Surely it is not necessary to go further than that in order for hon. members of the committee to see why they should vote against this clause. I have pointed out wherein I believe it is wholly unconstitutional, and with respect to this section, I should like to repeat what I said with regard to section 9, namely that I believe one of its purposes is to enable the governor in council to regulate the trade and commerce of this country in a way that will serve, if its policy is one of inter-imperial trade rather than world trade, to force the trade of the country into inter-imperial lines and to restrict world trade in other directions if necessary to accomplish that end. A policy of that kind up to the present has resulted in the trade of this country being diminished in very considerable proportions; to carry it further would destroy altogether what little trade still remains.

I should like to say just a word in regard to the constitutional question urged by my right hon. friend in the remarks he has just made. Surely section 91
of the British North America Act, which he has read in full to the committee, is in itself a complete answer to his constitutional objection. By that section the parliament of Canada is given exclusive jurisdiction to legislate in regard to the regulation of trade and commerce. This bill proposes to regulate in some respects the trade and commerce of this country, and in particular the export and import trade. In all constitutional discussions that have taken place since confederation, since the British North America Act was passed it has never been questioned that matters of export and import trade which constitute our dealing with foreign countries are specially within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament.
Parliament proposes in the bill now before the house to regulate the export and import trade and commerce of this country as defined in the bill. Parliament is the power which is legislating in this matter. If this bill is passed parliament merely enacts that the imports and the exports of the dominion may be regulated as provided in section 12 of this act. There is no attempt to take away, to alter, or to limit the power of parliament. The whole bill is drawn with the idea of utilizing the legislative jurisdiction which this parliament undoubtedly possesses under section 91 of the British North America Act which my right hon. friend has just read to the house. I cannot see anything in his argument. I think this measure is strictly in conformity with the constitution. If my right hon. friend's argument is sound our whole bill falls to the ground.	'
I think that anyone who appreciates section 91 and considers this bill in the light of it must absolutely conclude that this particular section number 12, is .within the jurisdiction of this parliament.
The questions of jurisdiction which have caused some difficulty in regard to this measure are not in regard to the regulation of trade and commerce as it pertains to exports from and imports into Canada, but I will grant you that it has not been the easiest thing to draw a line of demarcation as between dominion and provincial jurisdiction in the preparation of this bill. We have realized at all times that we were steering between Scylla and Charybdis, Scylla being the federal jurisdiction and Charybdis the provincial jurisdiction. But we believe we have been able to steer a course which does not infringe upon provincial jurisdiction on the one hand, or upon federal jurisdiction on the other. I want to take this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to bring forward a matter that has not been given the consideration it should have received in this house. Under this section the question of contracts and treaties arises. I hope the Minister of Justice will give me his ear for a moment. I dealt with the matter the other day at page 3121 of Hansard. I pointed out how impossible it is to conduct business to-day anywhere to any extent worth appreciating without making contracts and engagements ahead over a long period of time, for months and in some cases years ahead. Men may want their goods delivered at some far distant portion of the world and will ask: "Will you deliver such and such"- it may be telegraph poles, for instance, which have to be wintered or summered six months -"eighteen months from now?" Or a man may want fish or paper delivered in a certain place at a certain time and he often wants to make a contract for a long period ahead. A hundred instances might be given of these contracts arising to facilitate any form of marketing. But when this bill is passed they would hesitate to involve themselves in contracts because of the many penalties that may be involved. For instance, a ship pays a heavy demurrage each day that it is detained, and when men do not know under what obligations they may be under to some board when the particular time arrives, they will hesitate to make a contract. Take the case of a contract for flour to be shipped perhaps eighteen months or more ahead. ' The only answer the minister gave to my remarks the other day was this. He said:
I feel that all local boards will be anxious to facilitate all contracts rather than to break them.
But it is not a question of local boards wanting to facilitate contracts. Here are contracts in existence. When the boards come into existence, are they going to take no notice whatever of those contracts?
Let me show what they did in Britain. This is a parallel case because, of course, the same situation exists there. I refer hon. gentlemen to page 263 of the British Marketing Act, 1930-31, containing eight separate subsections. I cannot read them all, but section 8 provides carefully and clearly how all these contracts are to be taken care of. A man is not to be liable to a penalty for contravention of a scheme if what he does is in pursuance of a contract. I quite accord to the minister a desire to promote trade and commerce in Canada but I cannot understand how he can leave out such an obvious thing as that.
Again, no man knows better than the Minister of Justice how involved this is with the question of treaties. We certainly have over a score of treaties with other countries. Here is what the British act says. Section 3, which appears on page 475 of the 1933 act reads:
In deciding whether to make an order under this section-
That is the section where you have regulated importations of agricultural products-
-and in settling the terms of any such order, the boat'd of trade shall, among other considerations, have regard to the interests of consumers of the product to which the order relates (including persons who purchase that product for the purpose of subjecting it to any treatment or process of manufacture) -
We have taken no notice of that.
-and to the effect which the regulation of the importation of that product into the United Kingdom is likely to have upon commercial relations between the United Kingdom and other countries; and the board shall not make such an order unless they are satisfied that it is not at variance with any treaty, convention or agreement for the time being in force between His Majesty and any foreign power or between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and the government of any other country.
Obviously that includes any other British country. When we consider our trade relations with 'Great Britain under what we call the empire agreements and our trade relations with Africa, Australia and so on we should have regard to this matter. However, we seem to be going at this bill, so to speak, wide open. It is just like a horse that has run away with its rider; it takes everything in its course until it comes a smash. I regret that the leader of the opposition, when he was making his statement in regard to restricted trade since 1930, did not take a little time to make the picture more complete and accurate and -to point out that in one

That was the extent of our exports to that country in 1928-29, and by the tariff they placed against our cattle it was impossible to send any there in 1929-30.
Similarly with reference to our trade in milk, cream and butter going to the United States from the eastern part of Canada, during the right hon. gentleman's tenure of office through action taken by the United States our trade was restricted in one year to the extent of sufficient milk, cream and butter to be the equivalent of 52,000,000 pounds of cheese. That was the restriction of trade that took place before this party came into power. One could deal at length with restrictions in trade caused by action taken by other countries in regard to our wheat, but I feel that the facts have been put on record so often it would be a waste of time to deal longer with them.
One more point. There are some twenty-five or more countries at the present time that restrict their trade on the basis of quotas. We are living in a real world, and have to act accordingly. If, for example, the United Kingdom should decide to-morrow that we should not ship there in one year more than 20.000 head of cattle, how are we to deal with such a situation unless we have powers? That would be beyond the control of this government. The same thing might take place with any one of the twenty-five or more countries that have placed restrictions on imports. Everything would be haphazard if we had not power to restrict exports in dealing with countries that have imposed quotas. If the restriction that I have suggested were imposed by the British government as to live stock, what would be the effect? Every cattle exporter would try to ship every head of cattle he could at the earliest possible time, thereby tending to lower the price, and the result would certainly be injurious to our live stock industry.

Before this clause carries- and personally I hope it will not-I wish again to register my protest against this bill. I choose this clause as the occasion for my observations because I think it is one of the worst features of the bill. When we were dealing with the short title we expressed the hope that the government might bring down amendments that would improve this measure. They have brought down a series of amendments which may have improved it in certain particulars, but I think the sections we have been considering to-night, especially 9 and 10 and this one, are very bad indeed. A short time ago there was an interesting but perhaps too short debate on the constitutional aspect of this question. It has been contended that the regulation of trade and commerce belongs to parliament and that by this section there is an abandonment of that regulation. To, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) replied that if parliament has this power it has also the right to delegate it. I shall not discuss the technical point involved, but whether that is right technically or not it is certainly against the very spirit of the pact of confederation so to do.
Let us see how that will apply to another matter. Suppose when the Minister of Finance brought down his budget, instead of saying: We shall reduce the tariff on this item and increase it on another, and have special taxation of so much per cent, he should instead merely do as is done in this bill and say: We claim from the house the power to increase or reduce the taxes on any item we please during the year, without specifying the government's intention in the matter; that would certainly be contrary to the principles of confederation and responsible government. But what is not being done in the budget because it would arouse the whole country is to be done by this bill.
I know many importers in Montreal who are exceedingly disquieted by this bill. This section says that the governor in council may, by order or regulation, restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product. We saw a few evenings ago that natural products as dealt with in this bill mean practically everything produced in the country. The bill provides that the governor in council may make regulations for the licensing by the minister of importers. Now here is a man who has established a business in Montreal
or elsewhere-perhaps it has been in existence for many years, having been handed on from father to son-dealing with the importation of goods into this country. Import trade has met with great difficulties during recent years, as everyone knows. There have been wide fluctuations in the exchange values of moneys between different countries, and changes in the customs law which have been exceedingly complex and sometimes different between one office and another. By this bill an importer is threatened with the possibility that one day he may find in his mail a letter informing him that the governor in council, which means the government confronting us now, has decided that he is no longer to carry on his business, for some reason concerning regulation of marketing of the product, but that his competitor is to be given a licence to continue. Mind you, if he does not at once accept that impossible situation he is liable to be gaoled. A moment ago there was a discussion as to whether this act is similar to the one that has been passed in Great Britain. I think this difference has been made clear, that in Great Britain there is no pact of confederation, and that the Board of Trade is practically part of the government. But I will go further and say that if this has been done in Great Britain it is just as wrong as it is in Canada; that is my point of view. This government has not the right to inform an importer that because a board wants to market a product in a certain way he may not carry on his business. The government has not the right to do that, and parliament should not give the government that right.
I may express the hope now that this clause will not carry. This is one section that should have been amended. Here we have a long list of amendments; it has become the practice of this government to present a bill and then, a few days later, to present another in the form of amendments entirely changing the original measure. That has made very difficult the discussion by members of the opposition of any measure that has been brought down by this government. The principle is clear in this case, however; no amendment has been proposed. Here we have section 12, by which the government claims the right to restrict importations and to inform any importer that he must shut up his business. If he does not do so he may be put in gaol. I protest very strongly; I repeat that whether this is done in England, in Russia, in Germany or in Italy, it is wrong, and representing in a Canadian parliament a part of the Canadian people who
Marketing Act

are anxious to enjoy freedom of trade I do protest as vigorously as possible against the adoption of any such section by this parliament.

If this clause has any
virtue at all, Mr. Chairman, its only virtue is the effrontery and brazenness with which it puts on record the fact that parliament is going to surrender its power over trade and commerce in this country. I submit to you, sir, that the more one reads the section the more one is convinced that the government cannot have considered its effect before bringing down this measure.
In the first place, imports are restricted so far as they interfere with the marketing of regulated products, but the power to restrict exports is not limited to products which are regulated; lit is confined only to natural products. That is to say, the export of any product in this country, whether or not it is the subject of a scheme, can be regulated by the governor in council by means of a licence. I submit, as has been submitted by others, that this is not ,the sort of legislation to which this parliament should readily assent. I recall that under section 3 (e) of the N.R.A. in the United States provision is made for certain restrictions by the president with regard to the importation of products which are the subject of codes under that act, but even there the president is not given power to limit the importation of the products which are the subject of codes unless there has been first a reference to and hearing by the tariff commission with opportunity given those who are importers to present their case. As I recall it, there is provision for thirty days' notice as well. Where is the tariff board in this country? Two years ago the government passed the Tariff Board Act, and I understood that act was passed for the purpose of giving importers-and I suppose under this act it might apply to exporters as well-an opportunity of appearing and presenting their case, showing how the proposed regulations might affect them. The tariff board has been constituted, but there is no provision whatever here for any appearance 'before the tariff board by anyone interested. The governor in council may sit in the east block and make a regulation limiting the export, and may put an embargo on the importation, of any product which is the subject of a scheme. On the other hand they may sit there and require a licence for the export of any natural product, whether or not it is the subject of a scheme.
I submit that one cannot protest too vigorously in the name of the importers and exfMr. Rinfret.l
porters of this country, and those interested in international trade, against this wide and, as I said before, brazen attempt to withdraw from parliament and from the representatives of the people the right to regulate trade and commerce.

The long argument that has taken place to-night about substituting somebody for parliament has been

That principle has been acted upon by governments in this country; it was acted upon by the government of the right hon. leader of the opposition. The question of the principle is not measured by the size of the commodity with which it deals. I have not interposed in this debate; I do not desire to do so, but the other evening I listened to a very long and tedious argument with regard to the question of taking money out of the unappropriated consolidated fund. Just for the amusement of it I looked at section 7 of the Old Age Pensions Act, and that section provides that all the money this country pays for old age pensions shall be paid out of the unappropriated consolidated fund. That act was passed by the government of my right hon. friend. So, you see, the question of a principle is not measured by the number of commodities that it affects or the extent of its application; the question is whether or not the principle is legal and sound, and all the extravagant language that has been used does not detract from the fact that every principle contained in this bill has run the gamut of the courts and has been established by decisions of the court of last resort in this empire, the privy council.
